entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: As a slang adverb: slightly, secretly, or more than you openly admit (*I'm low-key stressed*). As an adjective: calm, quiet and not showy (*a low-key wedding*).
entries.usage: The adverb use is current slang among younger speakers (it spread from American usage), common in texts and casual talk, and often softens a confession or an opinion. The adjective sense is standard English and fine at work: *a low-key launch, a low-key person*. Keep the slang sense out of emails and anything formal.
examples: I'm **low-key** stressed about the presentation tomorrow, even though I told everyone I was fine.
We wanted a **low-key** wedding, just family and a few friends in my parents' backyard.
This new taco place is **low-key** the best food in the neighborhood.

drill.sentence: Don't tell anyone, but I'm {{low-key}} obsessed with this terrible reality show.
drill.hint: slang adverb, hyphenated: more than I let people see (not *kind of* or *secretly*)

entries.related: *kind of* — neutral, safe in any casual speech; *high-key* — slang for openly or very much, much less common; *understated* — the standard word for the adjective sense.

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: Genuine, honest and legal (*Is this website legit?*). In slang it also means really good, or works as an adverb meaning *truly* (*legit scary*).
entries.usage: Short for *legitimate*. The question *Is it legit?* about a seller, offer, website or email is used by almost everyone in casual speech. The senses "really good" (*This place is legit*) and "truly" (*I legit cried*) are slang, mostly among younger speakers, and too casual for work.
examples: Before you enter your card number, make sure the site is **legit**.
That email from "IT support" didn't look **legit**, so I reported it.
The haunted house was **legit** scary; my friend screamed the whole time.

drill.sentence: I thought the reviews were exaggerating, but this ramen place is {{legit}}.
drill.hint: genuinely excellent (slang, short for a longer word)

entries.related: *legitimate* — the full, neutral form; *sketchy* — the opposite, suspicious; *for real* — casual, also means *truly*.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Seeming suspicious, unsafe or dishonest, so that you don't trust it; also of poor or unreliable quality.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech about places, people, websites, deals and food: *a sketchy neighborhood*, *that link looks sketchy*. It expresses a feeling of distrust rather than a proven fact. In standard English *sketchy* also means *incomplete* (*sketchy details*), which is not slang.
examples: Don't click that link — it looks really **sketchy**.
The gas station off the highway felt kind of **sketchy** at night, so we kept driving.
The results looked great, but the preprocessing code was so **sketchy** that nobody trusted them.

drill.sentence: I wouldn't eat at that food truck; the chicken looked kind of {{sketchy}}.
drill.hint: doubtful, maybe unsafe to eat (informal; not *iffy* or *off*)

entries.related: *shady* — dishonest, more about people and deals; *dodgy* — the British equivalent; *iffy* — doubtful or not quite right.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To cancel plans or leave suddenly, especially at the last minute, so that you let someone down.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech and texts, especially about plans with friends: *Sorry for bailing last night.* Use *bail on* + a person or plan, or just *bail* (= leave early or cancel). It describes one event, while *flake* suggests the person is often unreliable.
examples: Jess **bailed on** us an hour before the concert, so we had an extra ticket.
The party was dead by eleven, so we **bailed** and went to a bar down the street.
Two of our four collaborators **bailed on** the project halfway through.

drill.sentence: Sorry I {{bailed on}} you at the party; I was exhausted and just needed to go home.
drill.hint: left you there suddenly (not *ditched*)

entries.related: *flake (on someone)* — similar, stresses that the person is unreliable; *ditch* — leave someone or something behind, often rudely; *cancel on someone* — neutral.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A decision or choice so obvious that it needs no real thought.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, business talk and journalism, usually after *be*: *It's a no-brainer.* It sounds confident and is typically about a deal, an offer or a decision with an obvious answer. It often takes *for*: *a no-brainer for anyone with kids*.
examples: Free upgrades for the same price? That's **a no-brainer**.
Moving our jobs to the new cluster was **a no-brainer** once we saw it was three times faster.
With rents this high, buying a small condo was **a no-brainer** for my sister.

drill.sentence: My company matches what I save for retirement, up to five percent of my salary, so signing up was {{a no-brainer}}.
drill.hint: a choice so obvious you don't need to think (informal noun)

entries.related: *an easy call* — an easy decision, also informal; *a slam dunk* — something certain to succeed; *obvious* — the neutral adjective.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To visit a place or person briefly, usually on the way to somewhere else.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech, at work and with friends: *I'll swing by your office later.* It suggests a short, easy visit with no formal plan. Use *swing by* + a place, or alone, often with *to* + verb or *and* + verb: *swing by and grab it*.
entries.pattern: swing by + place (to pick something up)
examples: I'll **swing by** the pharmacy on my way home and pick up your prescription.
Can you **swing by** my desk after lunch? I want to show you something.
My parents **swung by** on Sunday to drop off a birthday present.

drill.sentence: We're out of milk. Could you {{swing by}} the store on your way back from the gym?
drill.hint: make a quick stop at, on your way (not *stop by*, *drop by* or *run by*)

entries.related: *stop by* / *drop by* — same meaning, also very common; *pop in* — similar, more British; *drop in on someone* — visit someone without warning.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Seeming dishonest or possibly illegal; used about people, deals and businesses you don't trust.
entries.usage: Common in casual conversation and journalism: *a shady landlord*, *shady business practices*. Compared with *sketchy*, it focuses more on dishonesty than on danger or bad quality. In slang, *shady* can also mean secretly unkind or insulting, as in *That comment was shady.*
examples: The company had a history of **shady** deals, so investors were nervous.
Our landlord keeps part of every deposit and never explains why; he's a little **shady**.
Be careful with that dataset; it was scraped by a **shady** startup that ignored the site's terms of use.

drill.sentence: The used-car dealer refused to show us the accident report, which seemed pretty {{shady}}.
drill.hint: dishonest, as if hiding something (not *sketchy*)

entries.related: *sketchy* — suspicious, often also unsafe; *crooked* — clearly dishonest, stronger; *above board* — the opposite, honest and open.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To fail to show up or do what you promised, often without warning; *a flake* is a person who does this a lot.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech about friends, dates and coworkers: *He flaked again.* Use *flake on* + a person or plan, or just *flake*. It suggests a pattern of being unreliable, so calling someone *flaky* or *a flake* is real criticism.
examples: Mike said he'd help me move, but he **flaked on** me at the last minute.
Two of our study participants **flaked**, so we had to recruit more.
Half the people who RSVP'd **flaked**, and we ended up with way too much food.

drill.sentence: This is the third time she's {{flaked on}} our coffee plans; I'm starting to think she doesn't want to meet.
drill.hint: failed to show up again (stronger than *bail on*: it says she's unreliable)

entries.related: *bail on* — cancel or leave, can be a one-time thing; *stand someone up* — not come to a date or meeting at all; *a no-show* — a person who doesn't come.

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: I'm willing and happy to join in or do it; a casual way to accept a suggestion.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech and texts, mostly among younger adults. Use *down for* + noun or *down to* + verb (*I'm down to help*), or just *I'm down* as a reply to a suggestion. It is too casual for formal emails but fine with friendly coworkers.
examples: "Want to grab a beer after work?" "Sure, **I'm down**."
"We could rewrite the whole thing in Rust." "Honestly, **I'm down**."
She said she's **down to** help with the move as long as we buy pizza.

drill.sentence: "There's a free concert in the park tonight. Want to come?" "Yeah, {{I'm down}}!"
drill.hint: I'd like to join (slang; not *I'm in*, *I'm game* or *count me in*)

entries.related: *count me in* — same, neutral; *I'm game* — willing to try something, a bit playful; *feeling down* — sad, a completely different meaning.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something, such as a product, idea or event, that completely changes how things are done or how a situation develops.
entries.usage: Very common in tech, business, sports and marketing, and in everyday talk about small things that made a big difference (*This pan is a game changer*). Because ads overuse it, it can sound like hype in serious writing. It is spelled *game changer* or *game-changer*, and the adjective is *game-changing*.
examples: Noise-canceling headphones were **a game changer** for working in an open office.
For our lab, getting access to the new GPU cluster was **a real game changer**.
Analysts say the merger could be **a game changer** for the streaming industry.

drill.sentence: Once we started meal prepping on Sundays, weeknight dinners got so much easier; honestly, it's been {{a game changer}}.
drill.hint: something that transformed our whole routine

entries.related: *a breakthrough* — an important discovery, more formal; *a turning point* — a moment when a situation starts to change; *revolutionary* — adjective, often hype.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Extremely busy, with more work, tasks or people to deal with than you can easily handle.
entries.usage: Informal but not slang, used by all ages at home and at work; it's fine in a quick email to a colleague or even a manager (*I'm swamped this week, can we talk Monday?*). It's a polite, face-saving way to explain a delay or say no. Common patterns are *swamped with* + noun and *swamped at work*.
examples: I'd love to help, but I'm totally **swamped** with end-of-quarter reports right now.
The vet's office was **swamped** after the holiday weekend, so we waited over an hour.
Between the new baby and her night classes, my sister's been **swamped** for months.

drill.sentence: Sorry I didn't call you back; I've been {{swamped}} with packing for the move all week.
drill.hint: so busy I can't keep up (informal; not *busy*, *slammed*, *buried* or *overwhelmed*)

entries.related: *slammed* — similar, often a sudden rush; *snowed under* — same idea, also informal; *busy* — neutral and much weaker.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A casual way to admit a small mistake and apologize for it: *my fault, sorry*.
entries.usage: Slang common among younger and middle-aged Americans in speech and texts, for small slips like bumping into someone or sending the wrong file. It sounds light, so it's wrong for a serious mistake or anything that really hurt someone. In an email to a boss or client, write *Sorry, my mistake* instead.
examples: Oh, **my bad**, I didn't see you were waiting in line.
**My bad**, I sent you last year's spreadsheet; here's the right one.
"You took my charger again!" "**My bad**, I'll bring it back."

drill.sentence: "You just stepped on my foot." "Oh, {{my bad}}! Are you okay?"
drill.hint: admits a small slip casually, two words (not *my fault* or *sorry*)

entries.related: *my mistake* / *my fault* — neutral, fine at work; *oops* — reacts to a slip without taking the blame; *I'm so sorry* — for anything serious.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To contact someone by text, call or message, often to make plans or to ask them for something.
entries.usage: Slang common among younger Americans in speech and texts: *Hit me up when you're free.* *Hit someone up for* + noun means asking them for something (*hit him up for a ride*). It's too casual for work emails, where *reach out* or *let me know* fits better.
examples: I'm in town until Sunday, so **hit me up** if you want to grab dinner.
My cousin **hit me up** for money again, and this time I said no.
If you need a ride to the airport, just **hit up** Marco; he has a truck.

drill.sentence: I'm free all weekend, so {{hit me up}} if you're doing anything fun.
drill.hint: get in touch with me (slang; not *text me* or *call me*)

entries.related: *reach out (to someone)* — the polite work version; *get in touch* — neutral; *text someone* — names the medium.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The feeling or atmosphere that a person, place or thing gives you, often one that is hard to explain.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech and texts for most ages, and fine with coworkers: *The new office has a good vibe.* Typical patterns are *a good / weird / relaxed vibe*, *give off a … vibe* and *get a … vibe from someone*. Newer uses like *It's a vibe* (= it's great) and the verb *vibe* are slang, mostly among younger people.
entries.pattern: a good / weird vibe; give off a … vibe; get a … vibe from someone
examples: The café has a cozy, quiet **vibe**, so I go there to read on weekends.
I got a weird **vibe** from the landlord, so we didn't sign the lease.
The new manager gives off a relaxed **vibe**, and the whole team seems happier.

drill.sentence: I can't explain it, but the party had a strange {{vibe}}, so we left after twenty minutes.
drill.hint: overall feeling of the place (not *atmosphere*, *mood*, *feel* or *energy*)

entries.related: *atmosphere* — neutral, mainly for places; *energy* — similar, more about people; *feel* — neutral (*the town has a nice feel*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Of a person: completely exhausted, with no energy left after work, travel, sport or illness.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for all ages, usually after *be*, *feel* or *get*: *I'm totally wiped out.* The short form *wiped* is mainly American and sounds more casual; British speakers also say *knackered*. Fine with friends and coworkers, but write *exhausted* in anything formal.
examples: After a twelve-hour shift at the hospital, I'm completely **wiped out**.
The kids were so **wiped** after the beach that they fell asleep in the car.
That flu left me **wiped out** for a whole week.

drill.sentence: Can we skip the movie tonight? I ran a half marathon this morning, and I'm {{wiped out}}.
drill.hint: with no energy left (informal; not *beat*, *worn out* or *exhausted*)

entries.related: *beat* — same meaning, also informal; *drained* — emotionally or physically empty; *wipe out* (verb) — destroy completely, or fall hard.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A rough estimate that is close enough to be useful, though not exact.
entries.usage: Used by all ages and common at work, in meetings and casual emails, so it's one of the safer informal words in this set: *Can you give me a ballpark?* It appears as *a ballpark figure / number / estimate* or just *a ballpark*. *In the ballpark* means roughly right; a ballpark is a baseball stadium.
entries.pattern: a ballpark figure / number / estimate; in the ballpark
examples: I know you can't be exact, but can you give me a **ballpark figure** for the repairs?
The contractor's **ballpark** was fifteen thousand dollars, but the final bill was much higher.
"How many people are coming?" "**Ballpark**? Maybe forty."

drill.sentence: I'm not asking for an exact price, just a {{ballpark figure}} so I know whether we can afford it.
drill.hint: approximate amount, a term from baseball (not *rough estimate*)

entries.related: *rough estimate* — neutral; *guesstimate* — informal, a guess presented as an estimate; *in the ballpark* — roughly right.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Paid work or a small business that you do alongside your main job, usually for extra money or out of interest.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and media, especially among younger workers; it sounds positive and enterprising rather than slangy. It's fine in casual talk with coworkers and in personal-finance articles, but a résumé would say *freelance work* or *a small business*. Typical patterns: *start a side hustle*, *my side hustle*, *turn a side hustle into a full-time business*.
examples: Her online jewelry shop started as **a side hustle**, and now it earns more than her day job.
A lot of teachers in my town drive for delivery apps as **a side hustle** over the summer.
He fixes bikes on weekends; it's just **a side hustle**, but it covers his rent.

drill.sentence: Between her office job and her dog-walking {{side hustle}}, she barely has a free evening.
drill.hint: extra paid work next to a regular job (not *gig* or *business*)

entries.related: *side gig* — same meaning; *moonlighting* — working a second job, often secretly; *day job* — your main job.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Disappointed and a little sad, usually because something didn't happen the way you hoped.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech and texts among younger and middle-aged people, and fine with coworkers you know well. Use *bummed (out) about* + noun or *bummed (that)* + clause. It describes mild disappointment, so it sounds too light for real grief or a serious loss.
examples: I'm really **bummed** the concert got canceled; I'd been looking forward to it for months.
He was **bummed out** about not making the varsity team, but he's trying again next year.
My coworker seemed kind of **bummed** after the promotion went to someone else.

drill.sentence: We were all a little {{bummed out}} when the rain ruined our camping trip.
drill.hint: sad because of the letdown (informal US, two words; not *disappointed* or *down*)

entries.related: *a bummer* — a disappointing situation; *disappointed* — neutral; *down* — sad, not necessarily because of one event.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To suddenly stop answering someone's messages and cut off all contact, without any explanation.
entries.usage: Slang that spread through online dating and is now widely used by most ages, even in news stories about hiring (*candidates who ghost employers*). It's almost always critical and often passive: *I got ghosted.* Fine in conversation and casual work chat, but too slangy for formal writing.
examples: We went on three great dates, and then he just **ghosted** me.
The contractor cashed our check and then **ghosted** us for a month.
More and more job candidates are **ghosting** employers by skipping interviews without a word.

drill.sentence: She hasn't answered a single text in two weeks; I think she's {{ghosting}} me.
drill.hint: cutting off all contact without explanation (slang; not *ignoring* or *avoiding*)

entries.related: *cut someone off* — neutral, end contact on purpose; *leave someone on read* — see a message and not reply.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Short for *fear of missing out*: anxiety that other people are having fun or good experiences without you.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, texts and lifestyle journalism, especially among younger people and in talk about social media. It's said as one word, *FOH-moh*, usually without an article: *I have serious FOMO.* It's also used about investors who buy into hype, and it's too casual for formal writing.
examples: I only went to the party because of **FOMO**, and I left after an hour.
Seeing everyone's vacation photos online gives me serious **FOMO**.
A lot of people bought the stock at its peak out of pure **FOMO**.

drill.sentence: I was planning to stay home, but I got {{FOMO}} when my friends posted pictures from the lake.
drill.hint: anxiety about missing the fun (four-letter acronym)

entries.related: *JOMO* — joy of missing out, a playful opposite; *envy* — wanting what someone else has.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A deliberately bold or controversial opinion, often given quickly to get a reaction rather than after careful thought.
entries.usage: Common in American sports media and online commentary, and now in everyday speech among younger and middle-aged people. People often introduce their own unpopular opinion with *Hot take:* as a playful warning (*Hot take: pineapple belongs on pizza*). About someone else's opinion it can sound dismissive, suggesting the view is shallow.
examples: **Hot take**: the sequel is better than the original movie.
Sports radio is basically three hours of **hot takes** about one bad game.
His **hot take** on remote work got thousands of angry replies within an hour.

drill.sentence: Okay, here's my {{hot take}}: breakfast is the most overrated meal of the day.
drill.hint: a deliberately provocative view (not *unpopular opinion*)

entries.related: *unpopular opinion* — similar label, sounds less aggressive; *a take* — any opinion on a topic (*What's your take?*).

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To suddenly become very upset, scared, angry or excited, and show it in an obvious way.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, often in warnings like *Don't freak out, but…*. It works without an object (*I freaked out*) or with one, meaning to scare or upset someone (*Spiders freak me out*). Fine with friends and coworkers in speech, but too casual for formal writing.
examples: My mom **freaked out** when she saw the size of the spider in the bathroom.
Don't **freak out**, but I think I left my passport at the hotel.
The fans totally **freaked out** when the band came back on stage for an encore.

drill.sentence: When the smoke alarm went off at 3 a.m., the dog completely {{freaked out}} and hid under the bed.
drill.hint: got wildly scared and upset (not *panicked* or *lost it*)

entries.related: *panic* — neutral, about fear only; *lose it* — lose control, often laughing or angry; *a freak-out* — the noun.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To suddenly lose control of your emotions and start laughing, crying or shouting, unable to stop.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, and the context shows which emotion: *The whole class lost it* (laughing), *I almost lost it with the kids* (anger). *Lose it with* + person means to get angry at them; *I'm losing it* can also mean going a bit crazy. Too casual for formal writing.
examples: When the groom's phone rang in the middle of the vows, the whole room **lost it**.
After three hours in traffic with two screaming kids, I finally **lost it** and yelled at everyone.
She held it together through the whole funeral, but she **lost it** when she saw her dad's old jacket.

drill.sentence: The teacher tried to stay serious, but when the class hamster escaped during the test, she totally {{lost it}} and started laughing.
drill.hint: couldn't control herself anymore (not *cracked up*)

entries.related: *freak out* — panic or get very upset; *crack up* — burst out laughing; *break down* — start crying.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To do something extremely well; to perform brilliantly in a game, show, talk or exam.
entries.usage: Slang that is now common among Americans of most ages, mostly as praise or encouragement: *You killed it!*, *Go kill it!* *Killing it* describes someone doing very well over time (*She's killing it at her new job*). Fine in friendly work chat, but too casual for formal emails.
examples: You **killed it** up there! Everyone was talking about your toast after dinner.
My niece **killed it** at her piano recital; she didn't miss a single note.
Their new bakery is **killing it**; there's a line out the door every morning.

drill.sentence: Don't be nervous about the audition. You've practiced for weeks, and you're going to {{kill it}}.
drill.hint: do brilliantly (slang; not *nail it*, *crush it*, *rock it* or *ace it*)

entries.related: *nail it* — get it exactly right; *crush it* — same meaning, also slang; *bomb* — the opposite, fail badly in front of people.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To do something exactly right or perfectly, especially something difficult or specific.
entries.usage: Informal but not slang; used by all ages and fine in friendly work conversations and chat (*You nailed it!*). Compared with *kill it*, it stresses accuracy, like the right answer, tone or landing, more than an impressive show. The object can be specific: *nail the interview*, *nail the accent*.
entries.pattern: nail it; nail + the interview / the landing / the accent
examples: Your impression of my mom was perfect; you totally **nailed it**.
She **nailed** the job interview and got an offer the same afternoon.
The gymnast **nailed** the landing, and the crowd jumped to its feet.

drill.sentence: I've tried to make my grandmother's soup for years, and this time I finally {{nailed it}}.
drill.hint: exactly right, perfect (verb + *it*; not *killed it*)

entries.related: *kill it* — perform brilliantly; *get it right* — neutral; *hit the nail on the head* — say exactly the right thing.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Your usual, most reliable choice: the person, thing or place you turn to first.
entries.usage: Informal but not slang, used by all ages in speech, reviews and lifestyle writing, and fine in friendly work emails. It's most often an adjective before a noun (*my go-to recipe*, *the go-to person for tax questions*), but it can also stand alone: *This sweater is my go-to.*
examples: Pasta with garlic and olive oil is my **go-to** dinner when I'm too tired to cook.
Ask Priya; she's the office's **go-to** person for anything Excel-related.
This old denim jacket is still my **go-to** for cool fall evenings.

drill.sentence: Whenever we want a cheap birthday dinner, that Thai place on Fifth Street is our {{go-to}}.
drill.hint: the place we always pick first (hyphenated; not *favorite* or *usual*)

entries.related: *favorite* — what you like most, not necessarily what you rely on; *default* — the automatic choice, sounds more technical; *staple* — something you always have or use.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: A real, recognized trend, habit or phenomenon that people know about (*Is that even a thing?*).
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech and online, mostly in *Is that a thing?*, *That's not a thing* and *X is a thing now*. It often shows surprise or doubt that something really exists or is popular. Fine in conversation and casual writing; in formal writing say *a trend* or *a common practice*.
examples: Wait, people pay someone to stand in line for them? Is that really **a thing**?
Ice baths after workouts are suddenly **a thing**; my gym just installed three.
Apparently, birthday parties for dogs are **a thing** now, and my neighbor just threw one.

drill.sentence: My grandpa didn't believe that people film themselves opening packages, but it's totally {{a thing}}.
drill.hint: real and widely known (two words; not *a trend*)

entries.related: *a trend* — neutral; *a fad* — a short-lived trend; *a thing* between two people — a romantic relationship (*Are they a thing?*).

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Quickly or briefly; used to make a request or action sound small and easy (*Can I ask you something real quick?*).
entries.usage: Extremely common in casual American speech for all ages, at work and at home, usually at the end of a sentence to soften an interruption. Using *real* as an adverb is nonstandard, so write *quickly* or *briefly* in emails and formal texts. Many speakers say *really quick* with the same meaning.
examples: Can I ask you something **real quick** before you leave?
Let me run to the bathroom **real quick**, and then we can go.
Could you look over this text to my landlord **real quick**? I don't want to sound rude.

drill.sentence: Hold on, I need to grab my keys {{real quick}}; I'll be right back.
drill.hint: for a short moment, said casually (two words, no *-ly*)

entries.related: *really quick* — same, slightly less nonstandard; *quickly* — standard; *in a sec* — casual, very soon.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Much or far; used for strong emphasis before comparatives, *too*, and *more / less* (*way better*, *way too late*).
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech and texts, and common in relaxed meetings too: *way better*, *way more expensive*, *way too early*. Before a plain adjective it sounds like dated slang (*way cool*), so say *really good*, not *way good*. In formal writing use *far* or *much*.
entries.pattern: way + comparative / too + adjective / more, less
examples: The new phone is **way** better than my old one, and it was cheaper.
We got to the airport **way** too early and spent three hours in the food court.
There were **way** more people at the farmers market than last year.

drill.sentence: Honestly, the book was {{way}} better than the movie; they cut all the best scenes.
drill.hint: a casual intensifier before a comparative (not *much*, *far*, *so* or *a lot*)

mistake.right: The exam was way harder than I expected.
mistake.why: As an intensifier, *way* goes before comparatives, *too* and *more / less*, not before a plain adjective.

entries.related: *far* / *much* — neutral, fine in writing; *a lot* — casual, also before comparatives (*a lot better*); *way back* — long ago (*way back in high school*).

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A casual, polite way to say *no, thank you* when someone offers you something: you don't need anything.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, especially among younger and middle-aged people, with servers, shop staff and friends (*Want a bag?* — *I'm good, thanks*). Adding *thanks* keeps it warm. Some older speakers find it vague or too casual, so *No, thank you* is safer in formal settings.
examples: "Can I get you anything else?" "**I'm good**, thanks. Just the check, please."
"Want some of my fries?" "No, **I'm good**. I just ate."
"Do you need a hand with those boxes?" "**I'm good**, I've got it."

drill.sentence: "Would you like a refill on your coffee?" "Oh, {{I'm good}}, thanks. I've had three already."
drill.hint: no thanks, I don't need any more (casual US; not *I'm fine*, *I'm okay* or *I'm all set*)

entries.related: *I'm all set* — also polite, common in US shops and restaurants; *No, thank you* — neutral, safe everywhere; *I'm fine, thanks* — similar, a bit more neutral.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To sleep at someone's home for a night or a short time, informally and usually for free.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, especially among friends and family, often with *on the couch* or *for the night*: *Can I crash at your place?* It suggests a simple, unplanned arrangement, not being a formal guest. *Crash* alone can also mean falling asleep suddenly from tiredness (*I crashed at nine*).
entries.pattern: crash at someone's place / on someone's couch (for the night)
examples: We missed the last train, so we **crashed at Danny's place** for the night.
My brother's been **crashing at my place** since his lease ended, and it's been three weeks.
If the party runs late, you can **crash at our place** instead of driving home.

drill.sentence: My cousin's graduation is two hours away, so we're going to {{crash}} at my aunt's place instead of paying for a hotel.
drill.hint: spend the night, informally (not *stay* or *sleep*)

entries.related: *stay with someone* — neutral; *sleep over* — mainly about kids or a planned night; *couch-surf* — stay with different people for free, often while traveling.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop paying attention because your mind drifts away, often without noticing it.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, about meetings, lectures, long drives or TV: *Sorry, I zoned out for a second.* It isn't rude in itself, so people admit it openly to friends and coworkers. *Space out* means the same and is just as common in American English.
examples: Sorry, I totally **zoned out**. What did you say about Saturday?
The lecture was so dry that half the class **zoned out** after twenty minutes.
I sometimes **zone out** on long drives and can't remember the last ten miles.

drill.sentence: My dad always {{zones out}} when my mom starts talking about her garden.
drill.hint: lets his mind wander away (not *spaces out* or *tunes out*)

entries.related: *space out* — same; *tune out* — stop listening, often on purpose; *daydream* — think about pleasant things instead of listening.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be ready to support, protect or defend someone, especially when things get difficult.
entries.usage: Used by all ages among friends, family, teammates and coworkers; it sounds warm and loyal. The usual forms are *I've got your back* and the more casual *I got your back*. Fine in a friendly message to a colleague, but too casual for formal writing.
entries.pattern: I've got your back; have each other's back
examples: Don't worry about the meeting with HR; I've **got your back**.
My older sister always **had my back** when kids picked on me at school.
Good teammates **have each other's back**, even after a bad loss.

drill.sentence: If anyone gives you trouble on your first day, come find me. I've {{got your back}}.
drill.hint: will support and defend you (not *got you*)

entries.related: *stand by someone* — neutral, stay loyal; *stick up for someone* — defend someone who is criticized; *I got you* — I'll help you.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: I'll help you or take care of it for you; as a reply, it can also mean *I understand*.
entries.usage: Slang common among younger Americans in speech and texts, often written *I gotchu*. As a promise it means *I'll cover it* (*Don't worry about the bill, I got you*); as a reply it means *I see what you mean*, like *gotcha*. Common among friendly coworkers, but too casual for work emails.
examples: "I forgot my wallet at home." "Don't worry, **I got you**. Lunch is on me."
"Can you cover my shift on Saturday?" "Yeah, **I got you**."
"Turn left at the gas station, not at the first light." "Okay, **I got you**."

drill.sentence: "I'm twenty bucks short for the concert ticket." "No problem, {{I got you}}. Pay me back whenever."
drill.hint: a promise to pay for you (slang, three words, no *'ve*; not *I got this*)

entries.related: *I've got you covered* — same promise, more standard; *gotcha* — I understand, or I caught you; *I got this* — I can handle it myself.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A short phrase of encouragement meaning *you can do it*, said to someone before a challenge.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech and texts from parents, friends, coaches and supportive coworkers. It drops the *'ve* of *You've got this*, which sounds casual and warm rather than wrong. Perfect for a quick message before an exam or interview, but not for formal writing.
examples: Big interview tomorrow? **You got this**. Just be yourself.
Before the race, her coach looked her in the eye and said, "Breathe. **You got this**."
My son was scared of the high dive, so we all yelled, "**You got this**!"

drill.sentence: I know the driving test feels scary, but you've practiced so much. {{You got this}}!
drill.hint: an encouraging promise that the person will succeed (three words, no *'ve*; not *you can do it*)

entries.related: *You can do it* — neutral, a bit more childlike; *Go get 'em* — energetic send-off; *Break a leg* — good luck before a performance.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: As slang, so awkward or embarrassing that it's painful to watch (*That video is so cringe*). As a verb, to feel embarrassed for someone or about something.
entries.usage: The adjective is internet slang, very common among teens and people in their twenties; older speakers more often say *cringey* or *cringeworthy*. The verb is standard English for all ages: *I cringe when I hear my old voicemail.* Keep the adjective for texts and casual talk.
examples: My dad tried to copy a viral dance at our family barbecue, and it was so **cringe**.
I still **cringe** when I think about what I wore to my eighth-grade dance.
The company's attempt to use teen slang in its ads was pure **cringe**.

drill.sentence: Reading my high school diary out loud made me {{cringe}} so hard that I had to stop.
drill.hint: feel painfully embarrassed (not *blush* or *wince*)

entries.related: *cringey* / *cringeworthy* — adjectives, less slangy; *awkward* — neutral; *secondhand embarrassment* — feeling embarrassed for someone else.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Bitter, annoyed or resentful, especially about something small, like losing a game or not being invited.
entries.usage: Slang common among younger Americans, gamers and sports fans: *Why are you so salty?* It suggests that the anger is a little petty, and it usually takes *about*: *still salty about the game*. Fine for joking with friends, but too slangy for anything serious at work.
examples: He's still **salty** about losing to his little brother at Monopoly.
Don't get **salty** just because I didn't like your playlist.
Some fans were pretty **salty** after the referee's call in the final minute.

drill.sentence: She wasn't invited on the group trip, and she's been a little {{salty}} about it all week.
drill.hint: resentful in a slightly petty way (slang; not *bitter*, *sore* or *upset*)

entries.related: *bitter* — neutral, often deeper and longer-lasting; *sore* — informal, upset after losing; *petty* — caring too much about small things.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Too dramatic or over the top: putting much more effort, emotion or style into something than the situation needs.
entries.usage: Slang common among younger Americans and on social media, usually after *be*: *She's so extra.* It can be critical or affectionate depending on tone, and often describes behavior (*That's so extra*). Too casual for work writing, and less familiar to older speakers.
examples: He rented a limo for a first date? That's so **extra**.
My aunt is a little **extra**; she brought a three-tier cake to a small picnic.
You don't need to text me twelve times. Stop being so **extra**.

drill.sentence: Hiring a string quartet for your cat's birthday is a little {{extra}}, don't you think?
drill.hint: more than the moment needs, showy (one-word slang; not *much* or *dramatic*)

entries.related: *over the top* — neutral phrase, same idea; *dramatic* — about emotions; *a lot* — casual, tiring to deal with (*He's a lot*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Relaxed, calm and easygoing; used about a person, a place, a plan or an evening.
entries.usage: Very common slang among younger people and widely understood by older ones: *He's super chill*, *a chill night in*. Calling someone *chill* is a compliment: they don't stress or create drama. Too casual for formal writing; in a reference letter, say *easygoing* or *calm*.
examples: My new roommate is really **chill**; she doesn't mind if I have friends over.
We're not doing anything big for New Year's, just a **chill** night at home.
The office has a pretty **chill** dress code, so jeans are totally fine.

drill.sentence: My parents were surprisingly {{chill}} about me getting home late, as long as I texted them.
drill.hint: not stressed or strict at all (slang; not *cool*, *relaxed* or *laid-back*)

entries.related: *laid-back* — informal but not slang; *chill out* — calm down; *easygoing* — neutral, fine in any register.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To like something a lot or be very interested in it, such as a hobby, a style or a type of music.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech and fine with coworkers: *I'm really into hiking these days.* It suggests a strong, often current interest; *I'm not really into it* is a soft way to say you don't like something. *Be into someone* means being romantically attracted to them.
examples: My son is really **into** dinosaurs right now; he knows every species by name.
I'm not really **into** horror movies, so you pick something else.
She got **into** pottery last year and now sells her bowls at a local market.

drill.sentence: Ever since our trip to Japan, my brother has been really {{into}} cooking ramen.
drill.hint: a big fan of (one word; not *obsessed with* or *crazy about*)

entries.related: *be a fan of* — neutral; *be big on* — informal, care a lot about (*He's big on punctuality*); *be into someone* — be attracted to them.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To tease, trick or bother someone for fun, often by saying something untrue to see how they react.
entries.usage: Used by all ages among friends and family: *Relax, I'm just messing with you.* It's usually playful, but *Don't mess with me* (or *with him*) is a warning not to cause trouble. Fine in casual speech, but avoid it in formal contexts.
examples: Relax, I'm just **messing with** you; there's no test tomorrow.
My older brothers loved to **mess with** me by hiding my shoes before school.
Are you **messing with** me, or did you really win the raffle?

drill.sentence: He told me the bakery had closed forever, but he was just {{messing with}} me; it reopens Monday.
drill.hint: trying to trick, for fun (not *teasing*, *kidding* or *pulling my leg*)

entries.related: *pull someone's leg* — tell someone something untrue as a joke; *tease* — neutral; *wind someone up* — British, annoy someone for fun.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To ignore someone or cancel plans with them, often at the last minute, because you don't care enough.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech among all ages, and it sounds critical: being *blown off* hurts. It takes a person or an event as object (*blow off a friend*, *blow off class*), and a pronoun goes in the middle: *He blew me off*. Too casual for work emails.
entries.pattern: blow someone off; blow off + class / work / a meeting
examples: I waited at the restaurant for an hour before I realized he'd **blown me off**.
She **blew off** her chemistry class to go to the beach with her friends.
When I asked my manager about a raise, she kind of **blew me off** and changed the subject.

drill.sentence: We had plans for Friday, but he {{blew me off}} to go to a party with his coworkers.
drill.hint: canceled on me as if I didn't matter (phrasal verb with *me* in the middle; not *ditched* or *bailed on*)

mistake.why: With a pronoun object, *blow off* is split: the pronoun goes between *blow* and *off*.

entries.related: *stand someone up* — not come to a date at all; *bail on someone* — cancel at the last minute; *blow off steam* — release stress, a different meaning.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To leave a place or set off for somewhere; used casually when you are about to go.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual American speech, at work and with friends, often as a polite announcement: *I'm gonna head out.* It sounds softer and friendlier than *I'm leaving*, so it's fine with coworkers and even a boss in conversation. Use *head out to* + place for the destination.
examples: It's getting late, so I'm going to **head out**. Thanks for dinner!
We **headed out** at five in the morning to beat the traffic to the coast.
Most of the team **heads out** around six on Fridays.

drill.sentence: I've got an early flight tomorrow, so I think I'm gonna {{head out}}. See you guys next week!
drill.hint: set off from here (casual; not *go*, *leave*, *take off* or *get going*)

entries.related: *take off* — leave, often quickly; *get going* — need to leave soon; *head home* / *head to work* — go in a direction.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do something without preparation and improvise as you go.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech about talks, exams, recipes, trips and parties: *I didn't prepare, so I'll just wing it.* It can sound confident or careless depending on the situation. The past tense is *winged it*, and admitting you *winged* something at work can sound unprofessional.
examples: I didn't have time to prepare my talk, so I just **winged it**, and it went fine.
We didn't book any hotels; we're just going to **wing it** and see where we end up.
My grandma never uses a recipe; she **wings it** every time, and it's always delicious.

drill.sentence: I didn't study at all for the history quiz, so I'll just have to {{wing it}}.
drill.hint: improvise with no preparation (not *fake it*, *improvise* or *play it by ear*)

entries.related: *play it by ear* — decide as things happen, without a plan; *improvise* — neutral; *fake it* — pretend to know or feel something.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A disappointing or annoying situation or event; *What a bummer!* expresses mild sympathy.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual American speech, often as a reply to bad news: *Oh, that's a bummer.* It's for small and medium disappointments, so for serious bad news it can sound careless. Fine with coworkers in conversation, but too casual for emails to clients.
examples: The pool's closed for repairs all week? What **a bummer**.
It's **a bummer** that you can't make it to the reunion; everyone was asking about you.
Losing in overtime was a real **bummer**, but the team played great.

drill.sentence: "I lost my sunglasses at the beach." "Oh no, that's {{a bummer}}. Were they expensive?"
drill.hint: a disappointing thing (informal US; not *a shame*, *a pity* or *too bad*)

entries.related: *bummed (out)* — feeling disappointed; *a drag* — boring or annoying; *that's too bad* — neutral sympathy.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Too sentimental, obvious or unoriginal to be taken seriously, often in a way that's funny or embarrassing.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech about movies, songs, jokes, pickup lines and ads: *a cheesy love song*. It can be affectionate (*I love cheesy holiday movies*) or critical. It also describes things that look cheap, close to *tacky*.
examples: The movie had a **cheesy** ending where everyone hugged in the rain.
My brother still uses the same **cheesy** pickup line he's used since college, and it has never worked once.
The commercial was so **cheesy**, with a whole family laughing at a salad.

drill.sentence: He proposed with a rose in his teeth and a {{cheesy}} poem he wrote himself, and she loved it.
drill.hint: overly sentimental and a bit silly (not *corny* or *sappy*)

entries.related: *corny* — old-fashioned and silly, very close; *sappy* — too emotional; *tacky* — cheap-looking or in bad taste.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To get or arrange something useful for someone, such as a discount, tickets, a contact or a favor.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech, especially among younger adults: *Can you hook me up?* The pattern is *hook someone up with* + thing or person. Be careful with *hook up with someone*, without an object in the middle: it often means a casual sexual encounter.
examples: My cousin works at the stadium and **hooked us up with** free tickets.
If you need a good mechanic, I can **hook you up**; mine is honest and cheap.
She **hooked me up with** a recruiter at her company, and I got an interview.

drill.sentence: My friend owns a bike shop, so he {{hooked me up with}} a used road bike for almost nothing.
drill.hint: got me, as a favor (not *set me up with*)

entries.related: *set someone up with* — arrange something, often a date; *sort someone out with* — the British equivalent; *do someone a favor* — neutral.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To abandon someone or something you no longer want, or to skip something you were supposed to attend, like a class.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech: *ditch your old phone*, *ditch class*, *ditch the plan*. When the object is a person you were with, it sounds rude (*They ditched me at the party*). It also appears in news headlines about dropped plans (*City ditches stadium proposal*).
examples: We **ditched** our beach plans when the forecast called for storms.
My friends **ditched** me at the mall and went to the movies without me.
Half the senior class **ditched** school on the last Friday before graduation.

drill.sentence: I finally {{ditched}} my old flip phone and got one that can actually send photos.
drill.hint: stopped using and threw away (casual, one word; not *dumped*, *tossed* or *replaced*)

entries.related: *dump* — similar, also used for ending a relationship; *bail on* — leave or cancel at the last minute; *skip* — neutral, not attend.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: One problem or condition that makes you reject an offer, a plan, a purchase or a person, even if everything else is good.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in conversation, dating talk, business and negotiation, so it's only mildly informal and fine at work: *For me, a long commute is a deal-breaker.* It often comes with *for* + person or in *is not a deal-breaker*. It's spelled *deal-breaker* or *dealbreaker*.
examples: The apartment was perfect, but not having a washer and dryer was **a deal-breaker** for us.
He's sweet, but he's rude to waiters, and that's **a deal-breaker** for me.
The company wanted me in the office five days a week, which was **a deal-breaker**.

drill.sentence: I loved the car, but it had no third row, and with three kids, that was {{a deal-breaker}}.
drill.hint: the one thing that made us say no (not *a no-go*)

entries.related: *a sticking point* — an issue that blocks agreement, more formal; *a red flag* — a warning sign, not yet a final no; *a must-have* — the opposite, a necessary feature.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very excited and full of energy about something that is coming up.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech, especially among younger people and in sports: *I'm so pumped for the game!* Use *pumped for* / *about* + noun or *pumped to* + verb; *pumped up* means the same. It sounds energetic and a bit sporty, and it's too casual for formal writing.
entries.pattern: pumped for / about + noun; pumped to + verb
examples: The kids are so **pumped** for the first day of summer camp.
I'm **pumped** to finally see them live; I've had tickets for a year.
The team came out **pumped** after the coach's speech and scored in the first minute.

drill.sentence: The whole stadium was {{pumped}} when the home team ran out onto the field.
drill.hint: full of excited energy (sporty; not *stoked*, *psyched*, *hyped*, *fired up* or *excited*)

entries.related: *psyched* / *stoked* — very close, also informal; *fired up* — excited and determined, often before a game; *excited* — neutral.
